name: DIY braces with rubber bands / paperclips

lead: DIY braces means trying to straighten teeth at home with household rubber bands or bent wire, as a cheap alternative to orthodontic treatment. The goal is a straighter-looking smile.

The idea is that improvised bands or wire apply force to move teeth. Professional braces apply controlled forces that clinicians adjust over months. The appeal comes from personal accounts and home attempts, and no published research examines the practice.

paras: People describe wrapping or looping bands or wire around teeth to pull them together or into line, with no clinician involved and no set schedule.
It has not been studied. The orthodontic reference describes decay risk and relapse even in supervised treatment, and the practice is unsupervised.

web.title: DIY orthodontic treatment: a case study (AAO)

angle.text: People discuss improvised bands and bent wire as a low-cost way to straighten teeth without orthodontic treatment, aiming for a straighter smile. The idea is that home-made tension shifts teeth into line. It rests on personal accounts, and no research on the practice exists.

lead: DIY braces refers to attempts to move teeth at home using improvised materials such as rubber bands, floss, fishing line or bent wire, without a clinician's supervision. People try it to close gaps between teeth or straighten crooked ones for a better smile, often after seeing online tutorials.[1][2]

The practice drew media and professional attention in the 2010s, when orthodontic associations issued warnings about teens and children using rubber bands to close gaps between their front teeth.[1][2] Professional orthodontics, by contrast, relies on brackets, wires and elastics adjusted by clinicians, typically every 4 to 10 weeks.[3]

The American Association of Orthodontists (AAO) describes a 2018 case report in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics in which a small rubber band used on an 8-year-old's front teeth closed the gap in two days but slipped under the gums, leading to severe loss of supporting bone.[1] No controlled studies of the practice have been published.
infobox: Fixed braces adjusted by an orthodontist[3]
AAO urges people to see an orthodontist before any tooth movement[1]

paras: Fixed orthodontic appliances use wires, elastic bands, springs and ligatures to apply forces in three dimensions, and treatment is adjusted at regular visits.[3] Wikipedia notes that poor hygiene during fixed treatment can cause decalcification and decay, and that over half of patients show some relapse within ten years, which is why retainers are recommended.[3]

The practice can involve a rubber band placed around two front teeth to pull them together, or other improvised materials such as dental floss, fishing line, paper clips, pencils or homemade retainers, or pushing teeth with the fingers.[2] The AAO attributes the trend mainly to social media, with an orthodontist citing hundreds of tutorial videos on YouTube; about 70 percent of DIY patients in an AAO survey were aged 10 to 34.[2]

The AAO reports a case in which an 8-year-old boy's parents used a small rubber band to close a gap between his permanent front teeth. The gap closed in two days, but the band slipped beneath the gum unnoticed, destroying supporting tissue; X-rays showed more than 75 percent loss of the bone around the teeth, and the two front teeth could not be saved. Rebuilding a healthy smile took about three years and nine months of treatment. The case was reported in the December 2018 issue of the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics.[1]

The AAO urges people to avoid DIY braces and to see an orthodontist before any tooth movement.[1] An AAO orthodontist quoted in news coverage stressed that moving teeth is a biological process that should follow an in-person assessment.[2]

In a 2017 news report, the AAO said nearly 13 percent of its members had seen patients who tried DIY straightening, and an orthodontist described a patient whose rubber bands migrated into the gum and nearly cost her both front teeth.[2]
No studies found. The available literature consists of individual case reports of harm from elastic bands.[1]

timeline.event: A news report relays AAO figures and orthodontist warnings about DIY braces.[2]
